summary: This memo describes the encoding used in email and network news messages in several Japanese networks, which use character sets that need several bytes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: ISO-2022-JP lets email and network news carry Japanese text using 7-bit data. Escape sequences tell the reader when to interpret following bytes as Japanese characters and when to return to ASCII.

questions: how are escape sequences used in iso-2022-jp
subtitle: A 7-bit character encoding for Japanese text in Internet messages.

tldr.problem: Japanese message text needs character sets that cannot be represented as ordinary 7-bit ASCII alone.
tldr.mechanism: ISO-2022-JP uses escape sequences to switch between ASCII, the JIS Roman set, and two JIS X 0208 character sets.
tldr.outcome: The memo documents an encoding used in Japanese email and network news. It is Informational and specifies no Internet standard.

today: RFC 1468 is an Informational memo published in June 1993. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Background
sections.content:
RFC 1468 describes ISO-2022-JP, an encoding used for electronic mail and network news messages in several Japanese networks. It was first specified and used in JUNET and was also widely used in Japanese IP communities when the memo was written.

The name ISO-2022-JP is intended for the charset parameter in MIME headers. The encoding represents Japanese text while keeping message data in a 7-bit form.
sections.plainLanguage: ISO-2022-JP is an encoding for Japanese text in email and network news. It uses control sequences so the message can stay in 7-bit form.

sections.title: Switching Between Character Sets
sections.content:
A message starts in ASCII. The sequence ESC $ B switches to JIS X 0208-1983, where each character uses two bytes. The sequence ESC ( B switches back to ASCII, where each character uses one byte.

The memo also permits ESC ( J for the JIS X 0201 Roman set and ESC $ @ for JIS X 0208-1978. The Roman set differs from ASCII in its backslash and tilde characters.
sections.plainLanguage: An escape sequence tells the reader which character set to use next. Japanese JIS X 0208 characters use two bytes, while ASCII characters use one.

sections.title: Line and Message Rules
sections.content:
If a line contains JIS X 0208 characters, the text must switch to ASCII or the Roman set before the line ends. The next line begins in the set selected before that line ending. The entire message must end in ASCII.

A JIS X 0208 character must not be split across a line break. The memo recommends that users keep lines within 80 display columns, or preferably about 75, and notes that JIS X 0208 characters take two display columns.
sections.plainLanguage: Switch back to ASCII or Roman before ending a line that contains Japanese characters. End the message in ASCII and do not split a two-byte character at a line break.

sections.title: Declaring the Encoding in MIME
sections.content:
A MIME message can identify this encoding with a header such as Content-Type: text/plain; charset=iso-2022-jp. Because ISO-2022-JP is already in 7-bit form, the memo says a Content-Transfer-Encoding header is not necessary.

The memo also permits ISO-2022-JP in MIME Part 2 headers and says to use the “B” encoding there. Some systems may display certain escape sequences alike, but relaying systems must preserve the sequences exactly.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIME charset parameter tells the receiver to decode the message as ISO-2022-JP. Relaying systems must preserve its escape sequences.

sections.title: Status and Security Note
sections.content:
The memo is Informational and does not specify an Internet standard. It documents an encoding used by Japanese message systems at the time of publication.

Its Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed. The encoding rules describe character representation and message formatting.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1468 is an Informational memo, not an Internet standard. It does not discuss security issues.
